findings.claim: Ambulance transport from the beneficiary's residence to a hospital is a type of service the policy can pay for. Payment depends on the listed conditions being met, and the supplier's approved status is not shown in the case facts (UNKNOWN).
findings.quote: Patient was transported by
findings.case_fact: On April 17, 2011, the beneficiary was transported from her residence to a hospital.

findings.claim: The policy presumes the contraindication condition is met when documentation shows chest pain or cardiac distress. The ambulance report records chest pain as the reason for transport, which favors eligibility.

findings.case_fact: The ambulance report states that the beneficiary was being transported due to chest pain.

findings.claim: The case facts find that other transportation could safely have been used. Under the necessity rule, no payment may be made in that situation, so the core eligibility condition is not satisfied. This outweighs the chest-pain presumption, which is a presumption and not a bar.
findings.quote: In any case in which some means of transportation other than an ambulance could be used without endangering the individual's health
findings.case_fact: The beneficiary could have been safely transported by other means.

findings.claim: The policy covers inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF) care that requires multiple therapy disciplines, one of which must be PT or OT. The patient received PT, OT and speech therapy, so this basic eligibility condition appears met.
findings.quote: the patient required the active and ongoing therapeutic intervention of multiple therapy disciplines (physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, or prosthetics/orthotics), one of which must be physical or occupational therapy.
findings.case_fact: he received physical therapy daily for 60-90 minutes.

findings.claim: The policy requires a reasonable expectation of measurable, practical improvement within a set period. The patient was deemed a good rehabilitation candidate with specific functional goals, and he met his discharge goal of returning home.
findings.quote: a reasonable expectation that a measurable, practical improvement in the patient’s functional condition can be accomplished within a predetermined and reasonable period of time.
findings.case_fact: was referred by his physician for intensive therapy for which he was “felt to be an excellent rehabilitation candidate.”

findings.claim: The policy's goal of a safe return to home or the community is consistent with the patient's rehabilitation goals and his discharge home.
findings.quote: the goal of IRF treatment is to enable the patient’s safe return to the home or community-based environment upon discharge from the IRF.
findings.case_fact: He was able to meet the goal of being discharged to his home.

findings.claim: The policy requires the patient to participate actively in and benefit significantly from intensive therapy. The patient's functional deficits, therapy participation and eventual gains support this expectation at admission.
findings.quote: patient must reasonably be expected to actively participate in, and benefit significantly from, the intensive rehabilitation therapy program
findings.case_fact: A.D. had regained modified independence in his ADLs, was independent in transfers, and could ambulate and climb 12 steps with stand- by assistance.

findings.claim: The facts do not settle whether the rehabilitation physician made face-to-face visits at least 3 days per week, whether a preadmission screening was done, or whether the required physician certification exists. findings.quote: the rehabilitation physician must conduct face-to-face visits with the patient at least 3 days per week throughout the patient’s stay in the IRF
findings.case_fact: the physician had to titrate the medications on a daily basis due to large fluctuations in blood pressure, uncontrolled diabetes

findings.claim: The patient was expected to participate in and benefit significantly from intensive IRF rehabilitation, and the case facts show she benefited enough to live at home. This meets the basic IRF eligibility criterion.
findings.quote: patient must reasonably be expected to actively participate in, and benefit significantly from, the intensive rehabilitation therapy program
findings.case_fact: she clearly benefited sufficiently from appellant’s services to enable her to live at home with family assistance rather than in an institution

findings.case_fact: daily direct contact by a physiatrist throughout the patient’s stay

findings.case_fact: the patient received three hours daily of therapy services

findings.claim: The IRF goal of a safe return to the home or community was achieved, which supports the expectation of measurable, practical improvement.
findings.quote: the goal of IRF treatment is to enable the patient’s safe return to the home or community-based environment upon discharge from the IRF
findings.case_fact: had regained the ability to live at her daughter’s home with modified independence

findings.case_fact: The salient issues are whether the patient required a relatively intense level of PT and other rehabilitative services

findings.case_fact: The combination of the beneficiary’s condition, age, medical history and limited mobility created a very reasonable potential for serious complications

findings.quote: The home health aide visits at a frequency appropriate to the performance of the health related services would be covered
findings.case_fact: a home health aide visited the beneficiary five days each week, averaging 30-35 hours a week

findings.claim: Inpatient hospital care is a type of service the policy covers under Part A. The claim was billed as an inpatient stay spanning two midnights (July 27 to July 29), so the service type is within the covered category.
findings.quote: An inpatient is a person who has been admitted to a hospital for bed occupancy for purposes of receiving inpatient hospital services
findings.case_fact: The appellant billed Medicare for the beneficiary’s inpatient hospitalization from July 27, through July 29, 2005.

findings.claim: The policy requires a formal inpatient admission order from a qualified practitioner. The case facts show the beneficiary was admitted for surgery but do not show whether such an order existed, so this condition cannot be confirmed.
findings.quote: The order must specify admission for inpatient services.
findings.case_fact: the 71-year-old beneficiary was admitted to the appellant’s facility for surgical repair

findings.claim: Inpatient status turns on the physician's admission judgment and the medical record, not on length of stay alone. The contractor found the record did not support inpatient status, so basic eligibility as an inpatient is disputed and not settled by these passages.
findings.quote: Admissions of particular patients are not covered or noncovered solely on the basis of the length of time the patient actually spends in the hospital.
findings.case_fact: the “medical record did not support an inpatient level of care”

findings.claim: A stable condition does not by itself rule out skilled nursing coverage, so the denial reason that the condition remained stable does not settle eligibility.
findings.quote: Skilled care may, depending on the unique condition of the patient, continue to be necessary for patients whose condition is stable.
findings.case_fact: There were no skilled needs identified or provided.

findings.claim: Hands-on wound care by nurses is a covered type of skilled nursing service. This fits the June 2007 pressure-ulcer care, but not the diabetes-focused visits in the plan of care.
findings.quote: direct, hands on skilled nursing care provided to patients with wounds, including any necessary dressing changes on those wounds
findings.case_fact: provided wound care, including cleansing and dressing the wound

findings.claim: Skilled observation is covered only if the need is documented at each visit. The facts do not show whether this was done, and the contractor and QIC found no skilled need. Homebound status and physician certification are not addressed in the passages or facts, so eligibility cannot be settled.
findings.quote: The patient’s necessity for skilled observation must be documented at each home health visit
findings.case_fact: The QIC found that the home health services were not covered by Medicare because the nursing visits did not meet Medicare coverage criteria.

findings.claim: Intermittent skilled nursing visits under a home health plan are a type of care the policy covers. The case describes skilled nursing visits for assessment and teaching, so the service type fits. Whether it is reasonable and necessary is a separate question and is not settled here.
findings.quote: Needs Skilled Nursing Care on an Intermittent Basis
findings.case_fact: the 105 year old beneficiary required skilled nursing visits for assessment of diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, osteoarthrosis

findings.claim: A plan of care (POC) exists, but the facts do not show that a physician or allowed practitioner established and approved it, or signed it. This point is UNKNOWN.
findings.quote: Services Are Provided Under a Plan of Care Established and Approved by a Physician or Allowed Practitioner
findings.case_fact: While the POC describes the beneficiary’s diabetes as "uncontrolled"

findings.claim: The policy requires the patient to be confined to the home, but the case facts say nothing about homebound status. This point is UNKNOWN.
findings.quote: Conditions Patient Must Meet to Qualify for Coverage of Home Health Services.
findings.case_fact: the 105 year old beneficiary required skilled nursing visits for assessment of diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, osteoarthrosis

findings.claim: The policy requires physician or allowed-practitioner certification, including a face-to-face encounter, but the case facts say nothing about certification. This point is UNKNOWN.
findings.quote: Physician or Allowed Practitioner Certification and Recertification of Patient Eligibility for Medicare Home Health Services
findings.case_fact: While the POC describes the beneficiary’s diabetes as "uncontrolled"

findings.claim: Homebound criterion one appears met. The beneficiary needed a supportive device (rolling walker) to ambulate out-of-room distances when therapy began.
findings.quote: need the aid of supportive devices such as crutches, canes, wheelchairs, and walkers
findings.case_fact: at the time the physical therapy began, the beneficiary ambulated with a rolling walker for longer, out-of-room distances such as to and from meals.

findings.claim: Homebound criterion two (normal inability to leave home) is not contradicted. The record contains nothing suggesting she was other than confined to the home. Clinician documentation of taxing effort is not itself shown, so this point is only weakly supported.
findings.quote: There must exist a normal inability to leave home
findings.case_fact: There is nothing in the record to suggest that the beneficiary was other than confined to her home.

findings.claim: The service type is covered. Skilled gait training by a physical therapist for a patient with a skeletal/muscular impairment is a covered type of care, and the visit notes show it occurred at each visit.
findings.quote: constitute skilled physical therapy and are considered reasonable and necessary if they can be expected to materially improve
findings.case_fact: The physical therapy visit notes reflect that skilled gait training occurred during each visit.

findings.claim: The case facts mention a Home Health Certification and Plan of Care, but they do not state that a physician or allowed practitioner certified homebound status. That specific certification element is therefore UNKNOWN. A physician order for therapy is documented.
findings.quote: the law requires that a physician or allowed practitioner certify in all cases that the patient is confined to his/her home
findings.case_fact: the “Home Health Certification and Plan of Care” reflects that the beneficiary experienced an exacerbation of arthritis
